title: Electric Streams
subtitle: Durable, replayable HTTP streams for agents and real-time data
throughline: One event travels from a producer's POST through the durable append-only log to a consumer that replays it from any offset and then tails it live.

chapters.title: A Stream Is a URL
chapters.blurb: Create a stream with PUT, append one event with POST, read it back with GET, and check or close it on the same URL.

steps.title: A Stream Is a URL
steps.coverSubtitle: One event's PUT, POST, GET lifecycle on a single address
steps.displayNarration: A **stream** is a URL-addressable, append-only, durable sequence of bytes. We follow one event from creation to readout.
steps.spoken: A durable stream is just a URL you can write to and read from. Let's follow one single event, from the moment its stream is created to the moment a reader gets it back.

steps.title: Create the stream
steps.displayNarration: Each stream lives at its own URL. A **`PUT`** to `/v1/stream/hello` on `durable-streams-server dev` creates it; PUT is idempotent, so re-creating with the same config returns `200 OK`.
steps.spoken: Every stream lives at its own URL. To begin, the producer sends a PUT to the path slash v1 slash stream slash hello on the durable streams server. That PUT creates the stream, and because it's idempotent, doing it again just returns two hundred OK.

steps.title: Append one event
steps.displayNarration: The producer appends the event with a **`POST`**. The server writes it to the end of the stream's **append-only log** — once written at a position, the bytes never change.
steps.spoken: Now the producer appends our event with a POST. The server writes those bytes onto the end of the stream's append-only log. Once data lands at a position, it never changes; new data can only be added to the end.

steps.title: Where the event landed
steps.displayNarration: The append response carries a **`Stream-Next-Offset`** header — the position to read from next. The event now has a durable home on the log.
steps.spoken: The server answers the append with a header called stream next offset. That value marks where the next read should begin. Our event now has a durable, ordered home on the log.

steps.title: Read it back
steps.displayNarration: A **consumer** reads the event with **`GET /v1/stream/hello?offset=-1`**. The server serves the bytes straight from the durable log.
steps.spoken: Now a consumer reads the event back with a GET, passing offset minus one to start from the very beginning. The server pulls the bytes from the durable log and hands them over.

steps.title: Peek and close
steps.displayNarration: **`HEAD`** returns metadata without a body — existence, tail offset, closure. A **`POST`** with `Stream-Closed: true` signals EOF; closure is durable and monotonic.
steps.spoken: The same URL supports the rest of the lifecycle. A HEAD request returns metadata with no body, like the tail offset and whether the stream is closed. And a POST carrying the stream closed header signals end of file; once closed, a stream stays closed.

steps.title: One URL, six verbs
steps.displayNarration: One URL, six operations: **`PUT`** create, **`POST`** append, **`GET`** read, **`HEAD`** metadata, **`POST`** close, **`DELETE`** remove. The event made the full round trip.
steps.spoken: So a single URL carries the whole story: PUT to create, POST to append, GET to read, HEAD for metadata, a closing POST for end of file, and DELETE to remove. Our one event made the round trip from producer to log to consumer.

chapters.title: Offsets and the Read Loop
chapters.blurb: Offsets are opaque, sortable cursors; the read loop catches up via Stream-Next-Offset until up-to-date or closed, and survives 410 Gone.

steps.title: Offsets and the Read Loop
steps.coverSubtitle: Catch-up reads, resume tokens, up-to-date, closed, and 410 Gone
steps.displayNarration: Every position is an **offset** — an opaque, lexicographically sortable string. The read loop walks them from the beginning to the tail.
steps.spoken: Every position in a stream is named by an offset. Let's follow our consumer as it catches up from the beginning of the log, one offset at a time, until it reaches the tail.

steps.title: Offsets are opaque tokens
steps.displayNarration: An **offset** is an opaque string you never parse. They are *lexicographically sortable*, with sentinels **`-1`** for the beginning and **`now`** for the tail.
steps.spoken: An offset is an opaque string. You never parse it or guess its format; you just hold the value the server gave you. Two sentinels matter: minus one means the beginning of the stream, and the word now means the current tail.

steps.title: Catch-up read
steps.displayNarration: Starting at **`offset=-1`**, the server returns all available data so far. Our event is in this batch, replayed from the durable log.
steps.spoken: Starting at offset minus one, the server returns every byte available so far, replaying the whole history. Our original event rides back in this first batch, read straight from the durable log.

steps.title: Stream-Next-Offset resumes
steps.displayNarration: Each response carries **`Stream-Next-Offset`**. Store it and pass it on the next **`GET`** to resume exactly where you left off — the heart of the read loop.
steps.spoken: Each response carries a stream next offset header. The consumer stores that token and passes it on the next GET, so it always resumes exactly where it left off. That single value is the heart of the read loop.

steps.title: Up-to-date and closed
steps.displayNarration: **`Stream-Up-To-Date: true`** means you've consumed everything *right now*; more may arrive later. **`Stream-Closed: true`** means EOF — no more data, ever.
steps.spoken: Two headers tell the loop when to stop. Stream up to date means you've consumed everything available right now, though more may be appended later. Stream closed means the stream is permanently finished; that's end of file, and the loop breaks.

steps.title: 410 Gone on old offsets
steps.displayNarration: Servers may run a **retention policy** that drops old data. Requesting a discarded offset returns **`410 Gone`** — recover by resetting to `-1` or `now`.
steps.spoken: There's one more case to handle. Servers may run a retention policy that discards data older than some threshold. If the consumer asks for an offset that's already been dropped, the server replies four ten Gone. The fix is simple: reset to minus one, or skip ahead to now.

steps.title: The loop in one breath
steps.displayNarration: GET, process, take **`Stream-Next-Offset`**, repeat — break on **`Stream-Closed`**, switch to live on **`Stream-Up-To-Date`**, recover from **`410 Gone`**.
steps.spoken: So the read loop is one tight cycle: GET from an offset, process the body, take the next offset, and go again. Break on closed, switch to live mode once up to date, and recover from a gone response. That loop carried our event all the way to the tail.

chapters.title: Idempotent Producers
chapters.blurb: Producer-Id, Epoch and Seq give exactly-once writes: duplicate seqs dedup to 204, and a new epoch fences out zombie producers with 403.

steps.title: Idempotent Producers
steps.coverSubtitle: Exactly-once writes, dedup, and zombie fencing by epoch
steps.displayNarration: Retries are inevitable. Three headers — **`Producer-Id`**, **`Producer-Epoch`**, **`Producer-Seq`** — make appending our event exactly-once.
steps.spoken: Networks fail and clients retry, so the same event can get sent twice. Let's make appending our event exactly once, using three small headers that a producer attaches to every write.

steps.title: Three headers identify a write
steps.displayNarration: A producer attaches **`Producer-Id`** (stable identity), **`Producer-Epoch`** (a session), and **`Producer-Seq`** (a per-request counter). All three together, or none.
steps.spoken: An idempotent producer attaches three headers to each POST. Producer id is a stable name for the producer. Producer epoch marks a session. And producer sequence is a counter that climbs by one with every request. You provide all three together, or none at all.

steps.title: The server tracks last seq
steps.displayNarration: The server remembers the last accepted sequence for each **`(stream, producerId, epoch)`** tuple, then appends our event once to the log.
steps.spoken: The server keeps a small record of the last sequence number it accepted for each combination of stream, producer id, and epoch. Our event's sequence is new, so the server appends it to the log exactly once.

steps.title: Duplicate seq dedups to 204
steps.displayNarration: A retry resends the same **`Producer-Seq`**. The server has already seen it, so it returns **`204 No Content`** without writing again — safe retries, no duplicates.
steps.spoken: Now the retry arrives, carrying the very same sequence number. The server checks its tracker, sees it has already accepted that sequence, and returns two oh four No Content without writing again. The data was already there, so retries are perfectly safe.

steps.title: Restart bumps the epoch
steps.displayNarration: On restart, a producer **increments its epoch** and resets **`Producer-Seq`** to 0. The server accepts the new epoch as the live session.
steps.spoken: Suppose the producer crashes and restarts. It increments its epoch and resets its sequence back to zero. The server accepts that higher epoch and treats it as the new, live session for this producer.

steps.title: Zombies get 403 Forbidden
steps.displayNarration: A **stale producer** on the old epoch tries to write. The server **fences it out** with **`403 Forbidden`**, blocking zombie duplicates after a crash.
steps.spoken: But what about the old, crashed instance that didn't quite die? If that stale producer wakes up and writes on its old epoch, the server fences it out with four oh three Forbidden. That's how epochs stop a zombie producer from writing duplicate data after a restart.

steps.title: Exactly-once, fenced
steps.displayNarration: **`Producer-Seq`** dedups retries to `204`; a bumped **`Producer-Epoch`** fences zombies with `403`. Our event lands on the log exactly once.
steps.spoken: Put together, the sequence number dedups retries down to a two oh four, and a bumped epoch fences out zombies with a four oh three. Whatever the network does, our one event lands on the durable log exactly once.

chapters.title: Live Modes
chapters.blurb: Once caught up, tail the stream: long-poll holds the request open, or SSE streams data and control events and reconnects roughly every 60 seconds.

steps.title: Live Modes
steps.coverSubtitle: Tail the tail: long-poll versus SSE, control events, ~60s reconnect
steps.displayNarration: Caught up at the tail, our consumer subscribes to *new* data in real time — by long-poll, or by **SSE**.
steps.spoken: Our consumer has caught up to the tail. Now it wants the next event the instant it's written. Let's switch from catch-up reads into live mode, where the consumer tails the stream in real time.

steps.title: Subscribe at the tail
steps.displayNarration: After **`Stream-Up-To-Date`**, the consumer re-issues its **`GET`** with a `live` parameter to subscribe to whatever comes next.
steps.spoken: Once a read comes back up to date, the consumer re-issues its GET, this time adding a live parameter. That turns a normal read into a subscription for whatever gets appended next.

steps.title: Long-poll holds the request
steps.displayNarration: With **`?live=long-poll`**, the server holds the connection open: **`200 OK`** when new data arrives, or **`204 No Content`** on timeout — retry with the same offset.
steps.spoken: The first mode is long poll. With live equals long poll, the server simply holds the connection open until new data shows up. If our event arrives, it answers two hundred OK with the data. If the timer expires first, it answers two oh four, and the consumer just retries with the same offset.

steps.title: SSE streams events
steps.displayNarration: With **`?live=sse`**, the server opens a `text/event-stream`. **`data`** events carry the payload, so our event flows down the channel as it lands.
steps.spoken: The second mode is server sent events, or S S E. With live equals s s e, the server opens a long lived event stream. Data events carry the payload, so the moment our event is appended, it flows straight down the channel to the consumer.

steps.title: Control events carry metadata
steps.displayNarration: Alongside payloads, **`control`** events carry **`streamNextOffset`**, **`upToDate`** and **`streamClosed`** — the cursor and state, out of band from the data.
steps.spoken: Interleaved with the payloads, the s s e stream also emits control events. These carry metadata: the next offset to resume from, whether you're up to date, and whether the stream has closed. So state travels alongside the data, but on its own kind of event.

steps.title: Reconnect roughly every 60s
steps.displayNarration: The server closes SSE connections about **every 60 seconds** for CDN collapsing. Clients reconnect using the last **`streamNextOffset`** — unless **`streamClosed`** is set.
steps.spoken: To help content delivery networks collapse connections, the server deliberately closes each s s e stream about every sixty seconds. The client just reconnects, resuming from the last next offset it saw. And if a control event ever says the stream is closed, the client stops and does not reconnect.

steps.title: Two ways to tail
steps.displayNarration: Long-poll: simple request/response, great for binary. SSE: continuous **`data`** + **`control`** events for JSON and text. Both tail the same stream.
steps.spoken: So there are two ways to tail. Long poll is simple request and response, and it works well for binary content. S s e gives a continuous flow of data and control events, ideal for JSON and text. Both tail the very same stream, and both deliver our event live.

chapters.title: CDN Fan-out
chapters.blurb: Immutable historical reads cache with ETag and 304; live cursor collapsing lets edge nodes fan one origin connection out to many tailing clients.

steps.title: CDN Fan-out
steps.coverSubtitle: Immutable caching, 304s, and Stream-Cursor collapsing at the edge
steps.displayNarration: The same primitive scales: historical reads cache, and live tails **collapse** at the edge into one upstream — massive fan-out from one origin.
steps.spoken: Now the payoff. Because streams are plain HTTP, content delivery networks make them scale enormously. Let's see how our one event reaches thousands of readers from a single origin connection.

steps.title: History is immutable
steps.displayNarration: Catch-up responses for a given offset range never change, so the server sends **`Cache-Control`** and **`ETag`** headers — CDNs cache and serve them directly.
steps.spoken: Start with history. The data at any given offset range never changes, so it's perfectly cacheable. The server marks those catch-up responses with cache control and an e tag header, and the content delivery network caches them and serves them directly from the edge.

steps.title: Conditional GET → 304
steps.displayNarration: Clients revalidate with **`If-None-Match`** carrying the **`ETag`**. When nothing changed, the edge returns **`304 Not Modified`** — no body, no origin trip.
steps.spoken: When a client wants to be sure its cache is fresh, it sends a conditional request with an if none match header carrying the e tag. If the data hasn't changed, the edge replies three oh four Not Modified, with no body at all. That's a cheap revalidation that never touches the origin.

steps.title: Live cursor collapsing
steps.displayNarration: When many clients tail the same offset, the server hands out a **`Stream-Cursor`** they echo back. The edge **collapses** them into one upstream connection.
steps.spoken: Live mode scales too. When many clients are tailing the same offset, the server hands each one a stream cursor value, which they echo back on the next request. Matching cursors let the edge nodes collapse all those waiting clients into a single connection upstream to the origin.

steps.title: One origin, massive fan-out
steps.displayNarration: Our event reads from the **log** once, returns through one upstream, and the edge fans it out to every collapsed client — massive reach from a single origin.
steps.spoken: Here's the leverage. Our one event is read from the log a single time and returned over that single upstream connection. The edge then fans it out to every collapsed client at once. One origin read becomes a delivery to thousands.

steps.title: One event, end to end
steps.displayNarration: **`POST`** appends to the **log**, a consumer replays it by **offset**, tails it live, and the **CDN** fans it out — one durable, replayable event, everywhere.
steps.spoken: And there's our whole journey. A producer's POST appends one event to the durable log. A consumer replays it by offset, catches up, and tails it live. And the content delivery network fans that single event out to the world. One durable, replayable HTTP stream, end to end.
